sections.section_title: Marriage, Divorce, and God's Original Design
sections.summary: Jesus teaches on marriage and divorce, arguing from God's original creative design in Genesis over the Mosaic concession to human hardness of heart, establishing that what God has joined together no person should separate.

sections.section_title: Children and the Kingdom -- Who Can Receive It
sections.summary: Jesus declares that the kingdom of God belongs to those like children and that whoever does not receive the kingdom like a child will not enter it at all.
sections.relevance: The passage presents kingdom entry as contingent on a human posture of reception: 'whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it at all.' The condition 'whoever does not receive' implies genuine human agency -- the person either receives or fails to receive. At the same time, the child metaphor emphasizes that the kingdom comes as gift to those with nothing to offer, not as achievement. The combination of gift and reception holds together divine initiative and human response without collapsing into either pure determinism or pure self-effort.
key_phrases: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child will not enter it at all
the kingdom of God belongs to such as these

sections.section_title: The Wealthy Man's Question and Jesus's Response
sections.summary: A wealthy man asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life; Jesus tells him to sell everything and follow, but the man goes away grieving because he has many possessions.
sections.relevance: The passage presents a man who is given a clear path to follow Jesus and genuinely chooses not to take it. Jesus loved him and offered him the way, but the man's attachment to his possessions caused his departure. His choice is presented as determinative of his outcome -- he went away, not because God excluded him, but because he could not release what competed with God for his allegiance. The narrative treats his refusal as a real choice with real consequences for his standing before God.
key_phrases: he was deeply dismayed by these words, and he went away grieving
for he was one who owned much property

sections.section_title: The Disciples' Astonishment and Jesus's Teaching on Wealth
sections.summary: Jesus teaches that it is extraordinarily difficult for the wealthy to enter the kingdom, declares it easier for a camel to pass through a needle's eye than for a rich person to enter, and states that what is impossible with people is possible with God.
sections.relevance: The passage declares that salvation is impossible on the human side ('With people it is impossible') and possible only with God. This emphatic statement of human incapacity and divine power leans toward divine determination of salvation outcomes -- human effort, including commandment-keeping and moral achievement, cannot produce entry into the kingdom. However, the passage does not explicitly state that God unilaterally selects who is saved; it affirms that God alone has the power to accomplish what humans cannot. The surrounding context (children who receive, Bartimaeus who believes) suggests God's power operates through human reception and faith, tempering the deterministic lean.
key_phrases: How hard it will be for those who are wealthy to enter the kingdom of God
With people it is impossible, but not with God; for all things are possible with God

sections.summary: Jesus promises that those who have left everything for his sake and the gospel's will receive a hundredfold in the present age along with persecutions, and in the age to come, eternal life.
sections.relevance: Eternal life in the age to come is explicitly promised to those who have chosen to leave everything for Jesus's sake and the gospel's sake. The framework assumes genuine human choice -- the disciples chose to leave their homes, families, and livelihoods -- and connects that choice to the outcome of eternal life. The 'first shall be last' reversal warns that God retains sovereign authority over final arrangements, but the overall frame presents human sacrifice as a genuine decision that affects one's standing before God.
key_phrases: there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or farms, for My sake and for the gospel's sake
in the age to come, eternal life
many who are first will be last, and the last, first

sections.summary: Jesus delivers his most detailed prediction of his coming suffering, death, and resurrection in Jerusalem, specifying that the Son of Man will be handed over to chief priests and scribes, condemned, handed to Gentiles, mocked, spit upon, flogged, killed, and will rise three days later.

sections.section_title: James and John's Request and the Redefinition of Power
sections.summary: James and John request seats of honor in Jesus's glory; Jesus redefines greatness as servanthood and declares that the Son of Man came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many.
sections.relevance: Two elements bear on the question. First, Jesus states that positions in the kingdom are 'for those for whom it has been prepared' (v. 40), with the divine passive implying God has predetermined these arrangements apart from human petition. Second, the ransom saying (v. 45) presents salvation as accomplished by God's sovereign initiative through Christ's substitutionary death 'for many,' emphasizing divine action rather than human choice as the operative factor in providing salvation. However, the passage's primary argument is about the nature of kingdom leadership, and neither element directly addresses whether God unilaterally selects who is saved versus who responds in faith.
key_phrases: it is for those for whom it has been prepared
to give His life as a ransom for many
the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve

sections.section_title: Bartimaeus -- The Blind Man Who Sees
sections.summary: Blind Bartimaeus cries out to Jesus as Son of David, refuses to be silenced, throws away his cloak, comes to Jesus, and is healed and saved by his faith, then follows Jesus on the road to Jerusalem.
sections.relevance: The passage attributes Bartimaeus's healing and salvation to his faith: 'your faith has made you well/saved you,' where the verb sozo carries both meanings and the neutral reading explicitly identifies him as both healed and saved. His faith is presented as a series of genuine human choices -- persistent crying out, refusal to be silenced, willingness to abandon his only possession, coming to Jesus. The author deliberately contrasts Bartimaeus (who had nothing and followed) with the wealthy man (who had everything and left), making the narrative structure itself an argument that human response affects outcome. The neutral reading identifies this as the answer to the impossibility of verse 27: God does what is impossible, and faith is the human posture of reception through which God's power operates.
key_phrases: your faith has made you well
he began following Him on the road
Son of David, have mercy on me
throwing off his cloak, he jumped up and came to Jesus
